_about: Island lore research for Windward (gate 1: the 10 richest places). Research and data only; nothing here is wired into game code. Feeds docs/ALIVE-SEA.md (thing templates, place profiles, artifacts, mini quests). Facts and INVENTED hooks are kept apart: everything in `facts`, `landmarks`, `folklore`, `placeName` and `timeline` carries a source id from `sources`; everything in `regulars`, `secrets`, `rumours`, `questSeeds` and `artifacts` is INVENTED (marked invented:true) unless an artifact lists `basedOn` real finds. No real private person is named. Docs are fallible: where this file disagrees with an earlier doc, the entry says so. Gate 2 adds 15 more places; thin places carry only the eras that have a source (an era is left out rather than padded with invention). Merged with agent 3's parallel research (handover folder lore-handover, 2026-11-07): new entries light:Stångehuvud and the Käringön island row relation/10239114, plus selected new facts, landmarks and sayings in 9 places; items from there carry via:"agent3". Source URLs added to the registry. Validated by a port of agent 3's checker.

light:Måseskär.name: Måseskär

timeline.t: A pole mark (stångmärke) is built at the Crown's expense where a stone cairn stood: 18 m high, red-painted, with a white board pointing down as topmark.
The pole mark south of the light (Svarten/Sydbonden) is rebuilt and given an arm showing east-north-east along the sailing channel through the southern ('great') inlet.

Open iron pillar tower, about 21 m, with a second-order lens, made at Eriksberg in Göteborg and shipped in parts; keepers' house, outbuilding, cellar, a blasted stone-lined well, a boat harbour with a slip. Lit 8 October. The old pole mark is taken down.
Tower painted with white fields so it can be told from neighbouring lights by day.
Two signal cannons on carriages for fog; a coal-fired steam fog siren in a new machine house follows in the mid-1880s.
Hinneskär cairn just south of the light: white, conical, 4.8 m, built in stone 1878, raised after 1978.
Light electrified (it burned paraffin before). 1955 an electric motor replaces the brass clockwork and weights, so the light can be watched from the house.
A small white plastic lighthouse is built beside the old one; the old light goes out in August and fog signalling is automated.
The old lighthouse is lit again 1 to 8 August by enthusiasts of Svenska Fyrsällskapet.
Declared a state building monument 7 December; the foundation Stiftelsen Måseskär has used the old light and buildings since 1988.

The Svarten/Sydbonden pole mark south of the light is replaced by a stone cairn (built 1878, later rebuilt). Probably the same cairn as Hinneskär: both records give 1878 and a position south of Måseskär, but the identification is ours.

facts.t: No lighthouse and no pole mark yet. The repo's own research finds no documented sea marks in the region for 1700 beyond an undated stone cairn at Måseskär.
A stone cairn (stenkummel) stood on the spot before the 1829 pole mark; when it was built is not known, so its presence in 1703 is possible, not shown.
Before the 1860s Bohuslän had essentially only the Vinga and Hållö lights plus a lantern on the roof of Carlsten fortress.

facts.t: The only lighthouse with keepers in the game window in 1950: fyrmästare, fyrvaktare and fyrbiträde; manned 1865 to 1997. All the other lights in the window were unmanned AGA gas lights.
The light shows white flashes in 1950 (fixed red 1865 to 1887, white flashes after). Electrified in 1950; the brass clockwork and weights still turned the apparatus until 1955.
The iron tower (about 21 m) is painted white with fields; the lens was swapped for a third-order one in the late 1800s.
A steam fog siren in its own machine house (built mid-1880s) and one of the 1873 signal cannons stand on the rock; whether the siren was still used in 1950 is not established.
Slate roofs on the house, outbuilding and cellar since about 1900; small stone-walled plots show the keepers grew their own food.

After the Second World War the Allies are said to have sunk about 20 ships west of Måseskär at roughly 200 m depth (raised arsenic suspected to come from chemical weapons). Dates and ship names not found.

The 1865 Heidenstam iron tower (the first of its type on the west coast, 22 m by the nomination text) was lit on 8 October 1865 with keepers' buildings, a harbour with slip and a blasted, stone-lined well.

A red steady light with a 2nd-order lens burned crude oil through three wicks (12 nautical miles). Changed to a four-wick kerosene lamp in 1884 and to a rotating 3rd-order lens driven by a weight and clockwork in 1887. (Sources disagree slightly on lens order/year with sv.wikipedia.)

Two signal cannons on carriages were set up in 1873 for fog; a coal-fired steam fog siren in a new engine house took over in the mid-1880s. (IALA says a steam engine for a foghorn came in 1873 and a gong came first; the two accounts differ.)
1950: the light is electrified (power by submarine cable per IALA); in 1955 an electric motor replaces the clockwork and plumb-weight, so the light can be watched from the dwelling.

village:Käringön.name: Käringön

timeline.t: The island is written 'Kierlingøon'.
Olof Knape (later Strömstierna) is born on Käringön; admiralty captain 1700; ennobled; died 1730.

The Swedish squadron chief at the battle of Dynekilen (8 July 1716) is named as Olof Strömstierna, which matches the Käringön-born captain. The identification is ours: sv.wikipedia's Tordenskjold article names the commander, HSA names the Käringön man; no page says they are the same.
Church taken into use; the 1797 bell was donated by a fishing company on the island.
Korsholmen sea mark built: a white square stone cairn between Tornö and Vedholmen.

Early November storm: the bark Paula strands on rocks that are still called Paulapallarna; crew of 13 saved; a stranding auction on 12 November sold 800 sacks of rice. Several other ships are lost around Käringön in the same days (Nordkap 2 Nov, David with petroleum barrels 2 Nov, Queens Own and Martin Luther 7 Nov).
Tornö sea mark: a black cylindrical stone cairn, 3.5 m, on the island's highest point.
The bark Jupiter drives ashore at Korsets Stenar by Härmanö huvud between the Käringön and Gullholmen pilot stations; 3 dead.

The steamer Dora strands and sinks in the quarry sound between Vallerö and Tornö, later scrapped by Danes. (A steamer Dora is also recorded lost 11 December 1925 with a blown-up wreck; the two records probably describe one ship and one has the wrong year.)
Dredging in the harbour finds timbers of an older harbour structure in clay; a stock anchor from the harbour roads was raised in 1995 or 1996.

facts.t: A hamlet; said to be inhabited since the 1500s; the great herring period that 'put it on the map' only comes after 1747.
Its most famous son is a young sea officer: Olof Knape, born 1664, in the East Indies until 1697, made admiralty captain by Karl XII in 1700.
Nine-metre keel timber, stem knee and a plank fragment were dived up near Käringön; tree-ring analysis (1987) dates the timbers to 1516-1648, so a ship of that age lay on the bottom already in 1703.

Crews on Bohuslän boats avoided whistling aboard because it was thought to call the devil (later-recorded, from Skaftö-born painter C.G. Bernhardson's material).

timeline.t: Håkon Håkonsson's saga: the king put in at 'Hermanösund'; an unproven link to Gullholmen.
Fredrik II allows a Lübeck admiral to build booths at Hermanösund and Mollösund.
Oldest secure evidence of settlement: a letter mentioning a man 'paa Guldholmen'.
24 resident strandsittare (shore-dwellers) in the extra-tax roll; about 39 households by 1645.
The old fishing hamlet Härmanösund is abandoned.
Church finished in autumn (stands on Lilla Härmanö); altarpiece from 1828.
Hallgren cannery (later bought 1898 by a conserve company).
Dredging the harbour finds a large wooden ship's remains in its north part (ancient-monument Gullholmen 25).
Gullholmsbaden, a bathing place, is opened (Reso).

Early November storm: the bark Fata Morgana (timber cargo) is lost near Gullholmen, crew saved. Ship losses here cluster in storms (for example the galeas Rosina and Julius, both 15 Nov 1861), which shows how often ships came ashore.
A Riga-to-Hamburg ship with linseed cake is abandoned in a south-south-west storm and strands on Silleskär, Gullholmen.

facts.t: Best-documented place in the region: about 20 fishing families at the end of the 1600s, on crown land (kronoholme), free to build on.
A recognised anchorage: the Norwegian row fleet anchored here in the Gyldenløve feud; in the Great Northern War Tordenskiold called it one of the coast's most useful harbours.
The sound between Gullholmen and Lilla Härmanö was a harbour already in the Middle Ages (two medieval potsherds from test pits).
A now-vanished offering cairn (offerkast, Gullholmen 15) is recorded; a stone with initials and years from the 1700s and 1800s survives (Gullholmen 18).
Pilotage was carried on from the early 1700s; in 1729 two pilots, in 1736 two (Erland Nilsson in service 1721, Anders Pehrsson from 1724), in 1744 four plus two lads.

Dating: only one of three oak samples could be dated (latest ring 1717, no sapwood), probable felling 1727-1827, so the sinking falls from the 1730s to the mid-1800s. The museum says both Traung's mid-1600s dating and the Tordenskiold link can be dismissed. A treenail shows fire damage, so the ship may have burned. A separate 2007 Lund lab report on the 1930s finds gives only a weak hint of felling in winter 1752/53 and says more samples are needed.

folklore.t: The wreck in the harbour was said to be from Tordenskiold's fleet, lost in the Great Northern War. The museum rejects it after dating the timber to felling between 1727 and 1827, so the ship cannot be from 1700-1721.
folklore.note: The legend exists and the museum rejects it: both facts are high confidence. In 1703 the ship in question is not yet sunk; the legend belongs to later eras.

facts.t: Parish population 466 in 1950 (524 in 1940, a peak of over 800 in 1910); large-sea fishing 'was the base of the economy until the middle of the 1900s'; fish processing continued to the 1960s; about 150 houses and 100 boathouses in 1920.
Many of the island's houses became summer homes after the First World War; school and cannery closed (the year of closure is in conflict: left null).
The harbour wreck found in 1936 is an oak carvel-built ship, about 13 x 8 m remaining, dated by tree-rings to felling between 1727 and 1827.
Sold-off crown land: Gullholmen stayed a kronoholme until 1999.
In 1936 the harbour was deepened and the wreck pulled up; the head of the Gothenburg maritime museum Olof Traung called it a mid-1600s warship (press headline "a 300-year-old man-of-war").
Pilotage was withdrawn for good in 1915 (some sources: 31 March 1915); there had been a 1896 pilot house and a decked pilot boat in 1891. So no pilot station in 1950.
In the church a votive ship (full-rigged, by Johan Högvall) was donated in 1945, and in 1949 the pulpit evangelists were painted by Gunnar Erik Ström.

relation/10604591.name: Gåsö

timeline.t: Gåsö with the surrounding archipelago is bought from the Crown by two fisher-farmers for 50 riksdaler.
The galeas Ulrica sinks in 11 fathoms at Långesund in the Gåseskär group; anchor and cable salvaged.
'Bondeseglation' (farmer sailing) is encouraged; a few years later 17 ships are based on Gåsö; about 20 big sailing ships in 1860.
The big beach hotel (Strandhotellet) opens; a social house with warm and cold baths about 1900.
The island's former school, converted into a chapel, is consecrated.

facts.t: Occasional temporary households from the 1500s; the first permanent year-round residents come at the end of the 1600s.
There are stone-walled foundations (tomtningar) on Gåsö and Storön, walls that sheltered hunting and fishing and sometimes got a makeshift roof of oars and sails.
Skerries west of Storön are a breeding ground for harbour seals (knubbsäl) (a seal-protection area today); that Gåsö's seals were hunted in 1703 is not shown.

The Skaftö wreck lay on the seabed: a ship that foundered in the Lysekil archipelago around 1440 (found 2003 off Lysekil, excavated 2009 by Bohusläns museum, research led by maritime archaeologist Staffan von Arbin). It probably took on cargo in Gdańsk and was bound for Belgium: copper from Slovakia, oak timber and bricks from Poland, quicklime from Gotland, tar, roof tiles.

facts.t: After the great herring period Gåsö became a skipper community with about 20 larger sailing ships in 1860; steamships ended that, and the islanders turned to summer guests: a bath house around 1900, a guesthouse a few years later, the beach hotel in 1912.
Small-scale farming stopped in the 1940s and the guesthouse closed; the beach hotel closed about a decade later and the island shop in the 1960s; the school became a chapel in 1955.
About 150 inhabitants at the end of the 1800s; the older of two churchyards (about 70 graves, started in the early 1860s) lies a little from the village.
Wrecks recorded near the Gåseskär group include the schooner Orion (salt, 1829) and more from the 1800s.
Boat links existed with Gothenburg and Lysekil, sometimes Oslo when the steamer passed; year-round links to Lysekil and Grundsund ended in the 1970s.

Fiskebäckskil had its own municipal community (municipalsamhälle) from 29 January 1886 until it was dissolved on 31 December 1951, when the rural municipality merged into Skaftö. So in 1950 it still existed as its own unit.

Painter Carl Wilhelmson was born in Fiskebäckskil in 1866 (son of a mate) and had a summer villa with studio built 1911-1913; he died in 1928 and is buried at the church. The villa is still in the family and open to the public one day a year in summer.

In 1913 the church was lengthened by moving the chancel east, a sacristy was added and the tower raised (architect Charles Lindholm). The painted ceiling and walls date from 1783 (Joachim Gotthard Reimers); the hell scene over the west gallery was painted over about 1870.

Kristineberg zoological station was founded in 1877 on the initiative of Sven Lovén (Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences); summer laboratory built 1885, winter laboratory 1905. One of the world's oldest marine research stations, at the edge of Fiskebäckskil at the mouth of Gullmarn.

Klubban biological station (Uppsala University) is on Östersidan; at Klubban the remains of herring bins from the Bovik guano factory can still be seen (guano = fish meal fertiliser; tourism page, undated).

Östersidan: settlement began in the 1500s; in the 1800s it was a busy sea-captains' community, captains returning from long voyages built the larger houses; herring salteries, guano factories and canning gave work.

The settlement as it looks today began in the 1700s herring period, in three clusters: Ösö and Bovik on opposite sides of the narrow sound, and Värbo around Värbofjorden. timeline.t: Roskilde peace: Bohuslän (and Lysekil) becomes Swedish.
After big herring catches Lysekil is one of the six harbours where herring packing is allowed; a herring inspector is stationed. The herring period fades already in 1675.

Operation Bridford: fast gunboats run Lysekil to Hull with ball bearings through the German Skagerrak blockade, autumn 1943 to winter 1944; resumed 1944-45 with supplies for the Danish resistance.

facts.t: A fishing place older than the herring period 1566-1587, with its own church and priest; by 1645 82 adults, half of them strandsittare. Part of Lysekil parish from 1700.
The settlement lay round Norra hamnen (the old Gamlestan); in 1712 a Norwegian squadron was fired on there, so the village had seen real war.
A state pilot service existed from 1696 and compulsory pilotage from 1667; a pilot station by Lysekil is in the canon (Torhild's family) but no source for Lysekil's pilot station was found.
The herring boom of 1566-1587 and the 1666 packing licence had faded by 1675; the early 1700s were lean.

The pilot station at Lysekil was set up early in the 1700s ('inrättad tidigt 1700-tal'). A 1729 roll lists 4 pilots and 2 apprentices; the 1736 roll names a senior pilot, 4 pilots, a pilot servant and an apprentice; 1744 shows 4 pilots and 4 pilot servants. Nothing on the page dates the station more exactly than 'early 1700s', so late 1703 is not confirmed.

During the Great Northern War (1700-1721) the Swedish government sanctioned privateering from Lysekil's harbours. The English Wikipedia article gives no names or counts, and also says plundering of stranded ships was common on this coast.

facts.t: A town since 1 April 1903 with about 6,000 inhabitants (no 1950 figure found: 5,969 in 1960); engines, stone (declining), fishing, a bath resort since the mid-1800s.
Lysekils Mekaniska Verkstad (1899) made the Skandia hot-bulb engines; hot-bulb engines made in Lysekil until 1966.

Stångehuvud lay dark in 1950: its light was extinguished in 1940 and replaced by Stångholmen. The granite headland itself was saved from quarrying by Calla Curman and is a natural reserve (since 1982).
The war's last years made Lysekil a secret port: Operation Bridford ran ball-bearings to England 1943-45.
A great many wrecks cluster in the late-October storm of 1863 and the early-November storm of 1872 (see timeline of Käringön/Gullholmen).

Granite quarrying and stonemasonry were among the town's industries between 1850 and 1950; five granite quarries were working in 1909 and the stone industry stayed vital until the 1950s. Much of the stone went abroad (for example to Germany) rather than being used locally.

From 1859 Dr Carl Curman promoted Lysekil as a spa; the bathing establishment and cold-water bathhouse date from the 1860s, and Curman's two villas in Nordic 'dragon style' were built there in 1864-1890.

The pilot station kept buildings and boats through the 1900s: a new supervision house in 1928, a new motor cutter built at Ringens varv in Marstrand with a Skandia engine in 1941. In 1925 pilots and a crewman got 100 kr for rescuing the crew of the Danish schooner Merkur.

The combined lighthouse and dwelling was built in 1883; the light was in an attic room on the western gable and burned until 1938, when an unmanned AGA light replaced it a short distance north. A search summary elsewhere says the house held two keeper families (not fetched: low).
The western gable is painted white as a daymark from the sea; a stone staircase leads down from the cliff top to the site; the southern crack was used as a harbour.

Built 1883 as a combined wooden light and dwelling house by Bark & Warburg of Göteborg: the lens stood on the upper floor of one gable behind a row of windows; the sea-facing gable was painted white, the rest of the house red. Original optic: 4th-order drum lens with clockwork and a 26 kg weight, a two-wick paraffin lamp (replaced by a Lux light in 1912). The staff also tended the unmanned lights at Ösö and Fredagsholmen.

1938: a new concrete tower 425 m north, AGA light with a 4th-order lens, Bx(4) WRG 12 s, range 12 M, focal height 13.5 m, white 7.1 m tower; the old light was put out and the station de-manned. In 1948 the old station was sold to a private family (named on fyr.org; names not reproduced here).
The passage by Islandsberg is said to have a bad reputation: the sea outside is almost always unsettled and choppy. This second source agrees with the tourism page's "worst waters" saying.

facts.t: Quarrying at Stångehuvud began in the early 1870s; the Berlin firm Kessel & Röhl worked reddish coarse-grained granite at Stångholmesund. Quarrying lasted nearly 50 years in the later 1800s until Calla Curman's purchases.

The granite was shipped abroad, mostly as pedestals and columns for monuments in Germany, but also to Copenhagen, Amsterdam, Philadelphia, and (after 1910) as far as Singapore and Argentina. Loads left by ship from Pinnevik, Stångholmesund, Munkevik and Hästevik. About 5,000 cubic metres of facade stone for Vasakyrkan in Gothenburg were shipped in 1905-1908.

facts.t: Kessel & Röhl sold its stoneworks at Stångholmesund to Hebbel & Co of Uddevalla in 1904 after Germany raised import duties on worked stone.

Calla Curman bought most of the headland between 1916 and 1920 to stop quarrying. In 1925 (3 November per en.wikipedia) she gave the land to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, and the Carl and Calla Curman Foundation was set up.

The wooden light house at the western tip dates from 1890 and first burned kerosene; boys from Lysekil reportedly carried kerosene cans over the hills to the keeper. In 1917 the light was changed to acetylene gas (AGA), so no daily refuelling; Maritime Administration staff from Örholmen near Marstrand changed the gas tubes.

The light was put out in 1940, when a new lighthouse on a nearby islet took over its navigational role; the little wooden house was never demolished because it was so tied to the place. So in 1950 the house stands dark.

facts.t: Stångehuvud became a nature reserve in 1982 (en.wikipedia gives 22 March 1982, 47.15 ha; the county board page says 1983, ca 48 ha, so sources disagree by a year). The land is donation land owned by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.

The Curman Foundation added a solar panel, battery and dusk switch to power an LED decorative light at the light house in 2014; it bought the building from the Vikarvet society in June 2017 and renovated the roof and front.
The county board's rules forbid moving or removing stones, camping, motor vehicles and loose dogs on the reserve.
The light house was named one of the seven wonders of Västra Götaland in 2019 (en.wikipedia); two roads to the reserve were named for Calla and Carl Curman on 3 October 2020.
Some of the stone survives in buildings: Vasakyrkan and Kungsportsbron in Gothenburg, the granite stairs at Gula villan in Lysekil; ten columns of Jesuskirken in Copenhagen's Valby.

Käringön is said to have been inhabited since the 1500s; house foundations (tomtningar) have been found in the parish.

Olof Knape, later Strömstierna, was born on Käringön in 1664 (sv.wikipedia; en.wikipedia is said by the repo docs to disagree on birthplace). He went to sea in 1672, served the Dutch East India Company and the Dutch States for a time, and in 1700 got his commission as admiralty captain after helping Admiral Anckarstierna muster all seafarers in Bohus county.

facts.t: Käringön had a municipalsamhälle (local government for the built-up village) from 29 September 1886 until 31 December 1959; it had 568 inhabitants in 1900 and 548 in 1925.

The Käringön pilot station was still staffed in 1950 (it closed on 1 July 1960, its duties moving to Marstrand and Lysekil; staffed for at least 250 years). A new pilot boat was built in 1939 and the pilot house was moved and raised in 1926.

A lookout had been built on Vedholmen in 1880 to replace a condemned one; pilot families lived on the hill called Lotsberget near the lookout (the page does not say whether this is the later "Lotsutkiken").

The white wooden church (taken into use 1796) was red outside for about 100 years and is now white. The south entrance by the chancel was removed in 1952, so in 1950 it still existed. A floor clock from 1845 and the 1915 organ by Eskil Lundén are inside.

The preacher August Simson (1815-1900) was chapel preacher and teacher on Käringön from 1849 and had a vicarage built in 1877 at his own cost; it still stands, high up with a view over the island, run today by a foundation. He closed the island's illicit taverns, renamed families and was very strict.
A photograph of the Måseskär lighthouse and keeper's dwelling taken in 1940 (A. E. Johansson, Bohusläns museum) exists, for how the neighbouring lighthouse looked a decade before 1950.
